summary: Describes the registration policies for the .gov top-level domain used by U.S. government organizations. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 1816.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1811 sets registration rules for the .GOV domain. It defines which federal organizations qualify, how names should be chosen, and how agencies with multiple names should consolidate them.

subtitle: Rules for registering U.S. federal government names under .GOV.

tldr.problem: Federal agencies had registered multiple .GOV names without common guidance, and naming did not consistently follow the approved government structure.
tldr.mechanism: The memo limits eligibility, ties names to official agency names, sets one registration per agency, and gives existing multiple registrations a transition period.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1811 is informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 1816.

facts.label: Time to select a primary domain

sections.title: Who Can Register Under .GOV
sections.content:
The .GOV domain is delegated to the U.S. Federal Networking Council and is for federal-level U.S. government entities. State and local government agencies are directed to register under .US. The memo uses the agency list in FIPS 95-1 to determine which top-level entities and independent agencies qualify.

Autonomous law enforcement components of top-level entities are also eligible. Cross-agency organizations may qualify if they present a charter. Subsidiary, non-autonomous components, international organizations, and federally aided organizations are not eligible under these rules; Department of Defense subsidiaries use .MIL.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules reserve .GOV for eligible federal organizations. State and local agencies use .US, while some agency subsidiaries are excluded or directed to .MIL.

sections.title: Names and Registration Limits
sections.content:
A domain name should come from the organization's official name. The registration database should list the official name from FIPS 95-1 or the name in a chartering document. The .GOV authority provides registrations on a first-come, first-served basis.

Only one registration and delegation is to be made per agency. Each agency decides which part of the agency manages the domain space under that delegation.
sections.plainLanguage: An agency's .GOV name should reflect its official name. Each agency gets one registration, and it chooses who manages names beneath it.

sections.title: Transition for Existing Names
sections.content:
Agencies with multiple .GOV registrations could retain them for up to 3 years after publication. Within 6 months, each had to choose a primary domain; secondary domains had to stop accepting new sub-delegations and registrations. After 1 year, secondary domains would be undelegated. After 2 years, their registrations had to be mirrored in the primary domain, and at the 3-year point the secondary registrations would be deleted.

Existing registrations for entities not listed in FIPS 95-1 could remain subject to the single-registration rule, but no further such registrations would be made.
sections.plainLanguage: Agencies with multiple names had up to three years to consolidate them. Secondary domains faced staged limits before their registrations were deleted.

references.text: Federal Information Processing Standards Publication 95-1, "Codes for the Identification of Federal and Federally Assisted Organizations", January 4, 1993.
Postel, J., "Domain Name System Structure and Delegation", RFC 1591, March 1994.
